asDecan.p: Each sign is split into three ten-degree slices called decans, each with a planet and a small card. Your Sun sits between 10 and 19 degrees of Gemini, the middle slice, where the sign is settled in and at full strength, and the Chaldean order hands those degrees to Mars. Mars has no special dignity in Gemini. It's a visitor there, neither helped nor held back, so it takes on the tone of Mercury, who rules the sign. What you get is Mercury's quick mind with Mars's urge to have a go, and because Gemini is air, most of the fighting happens in words, or in your own head. The slice before yours is the Eight of Swords, Jupiter's, where the mind talks itself into a corner. The one after is the Ten, the Sun's, where a story gets taken to its end. Yours has the most push of the three. The Lovers is still your Sun card. This is the closer reading inside it, for your ten degrees.

You argue with people in the shower. Rehearsals, mostly, the thing you should have said to your manager on Tuesday, and by the time you're drying off you've won. Someone at a barbecue makes a slightly off remark about your job and you let it go, and you're still answering them in the car on the way home. A two-word reply from your sister gets four or five readings, each one a bit worse than the last. In company you're quick, and people like that about you, the joke's out before anyone else has thought of it. The trouble is the same engine keeps running after everyone's gone home. A long weekend with nothing booked is harder on you than a busy one, and by the Sunday night you've usually found something about yourself to go over.

Nobody expects it from someone who worries this much, but you're very good when something actually goes wrong. You've already run the bad version in your head plenty of times, so when the phone call comes, the car dies on the highway, a friend ends up in emergency, you're oddly calm. You know who to ring and what to ask, and you've usually thought of the thing everyone else forgot, the charger, the insurance details, the spare key. Mars was never much good at hypotheticals. Give it a real problem, with a form to fill in and a number to call, and it settles and gets on with it. There's a smaller gift alongside that, which is the jokes. Yours are quick and a bit dark, and in a hospital corridor or the kitchen after a funeral, that's often what gets people through the afternoon.

The worry doesn't always stay inside you. When you're wound up about something you can't fix, the money, a parent's health, a friend who's gone quiet on you, you tend to find something smaller to argue about instead. Your partner stacked the dishwasher wrong. A colleague's email had a tone. You go at it with a precision that's out of all proportion, and while it's happening it feels completely reasonable. Mars needs a target, and a nervous Gemini mind will hand it whatever's nearest. The other part is that worrying can feel like work. Going over a problem for the ninth time gives you the sense of doing something, and I've seen Geminis in these degrees lose a whole evening that way and still not make the one phone call that would settle it.

Bad news goes straight to your head. A redundancy, a break-up, a test result you're waiting on, and within the hour you've looked up everything there is to look up and read the worst forums on the internet. For the first few days you talk about it a lot, to anyone, fast and a bit too bright. Then about a week in the talking stops and the nights get bad. You're awake at two going over it, tired and snappy by day, and the people around you get the short answers and the sharp edge without knowing why, because by then you've stopped explaining. What helps is physical, which surprises a lot of Geminis. Mars wants the body used. A hard walk, a swim, a run, anything that tires you before your mind starts up again. After that, tell one person what the worry actually is, plainly, over lunch.

The Lovers is a card about choosing, and in love this decan chooses people who argue back. A bit of sparring over dinner feels like closeness to you, and someone who agrees with everything leaves you oddly restless by the third date. It gets harder when you're insecure. Then you go over the relationship like a lawyer would, the gap between texts, the single word ok with a full stop after it, the way they said goodnight, and you quietly build a case. Now and then you put that case to them at eleven at night, which almost never goes well. What most people don't see is how much you want to be talked down, gently, by someone who doesn't flinch at a sharp word. It helps a lot to agree between you that nothing serious gets raised after ten.

Work with an argument in it suits you. Law, journalism, sales, editing someone else's report until it holds up, fixing a system that's fallen over. You find the hole in a plan on the first read, and you're usually right about it. That's useful, and it also puts some people on the defensive, so it's worth learning which things to raise one to one and which in front of the team. Where you struggle is the waiting. A proposal sent off, a performance review booked for three weeks away, a restructure that's only a rumour. With nothing to act on, your head writes the ending for you, usually the bad one, and you can lose more sleep over an unanswered email than over a genuine crisis. This decan often does best somewhere that's never quiet for long, a newsroom, a busy agency, a support desk.

At twenty this decan often looks like a lot of nervous energy without much aim. Late nights, strong opinions, long arguments online with strangers, sleep that goes to pieces around exams or a break-up, and a feeling that your own head is the loudest thing in any room. By the mid-thirties most people with a Sun here have learnt something about their own wiring. They know the bad thoughts come at night and count for less than the daytime ones, and they've usually found something physical to do with the restlessness, running, boxing, a garden that needs digging. The sharpness gets pointed at work and at things worth fighting for. The fifties are usually a good deal calmer. People in these degrees often become the friend others ring at midnight, because they know that territory well and it doesn't frighten them much any more.

Keep a notebook and a pen by the bed. When you wake in the night with something going round, write down what you're actually afraid of, in one sentence, and next to it the one thing you could do about it and the day you'll do it. Then shut the notebook and turn it face down. In the morning, read it before you look at your phone. Most mornings the sentence looks smaller than it did in the dark. When it doesn't, do the thing you wrote next to it before lunch.
